options.text: Banks refused to make any mortgages at all after 2007
options.misconception: Banks cut back on lending, but they did not stop making mortgages entirely.

options.text: The government banned all home buying in 2008
options.misconception: The government never banned home buying.

options.text: Home prices rose sharply across the country
options.misconception: Home prices fell when the housing bubble burst.

options.text: Banks bundled the mortgages into securities sold across the financial system

rationales.A: Banks cut back on lending when the loans went bad. Cutting back is not the same as stopping all mortgages.
rationales.B: The government never banned home buying. Its response was to buy troubled assets and pass a stimulus.
rationales.C: The housing bubble burst in 2007, which meant prices fell, not rose.
rationales.D: The account says banks bundled subprime mortgages into securities sold across the financial system, which spread the risk far beyond housing.
rationales.general:
1. Ask how a housing problem became a financial problem. The account says banks bundled risky mortgages into securities.
2. Those securities were sold across the financial system, so the risk traveled with them.
3. When borrowers defaulted, the losses hit banks, funds, and lenders far from the original houses.
4. The table shows the human result: unemployment more than doubled from 2007 to 2010.
Remember: bundling a risky loan spreads its risk to everyone holding the bundle.

stimulus.text:
Data table: United States unemployment rate, annual average, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey.

| Year | Unemployment rate |
| 2007 | 4.6% |
| 2008 | 5.8% |
| 2009 | 9.3% |
| 2010 | 9.6% |

Paraphrase of a secondary account: In the 2000s, banks made risky subprime mortgages to borrowers with low credit ratings, then bundled those mortgages into securities sold across the financial system. When the housing bubble burst in 2007, borrowers defaulted, foreclosures spread, and banks holding the bundled loans cut back on lending.

In 2008, Congress passed the Troubled Asset Relief Program, giving the government up to 700 billion dollars to buy troubled mortgage assets from financial firms. In 2009, President Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, a stimulus of almost 800 billion dollars for infrastructure, schools, and hospitals.
